content: Seven percent of patients discontinued linezolid prematurely due to adverse events. Based on findings from the Nix-TB study, it may be necessary to adjust the dosage of linezolid during treatment to manage side effects effectively. This underscores the importance of close monitoring, patient follow-up, and adherence to adverse drug safety monitoring (aDSM) protocols. Additional studies, such as the ZeNix study conducted by the TB Alliance, are ongoing to determine the optimal dosing and duration of linezolid for treating drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB). However, the results of these studies are not yet available for review. The BPaL regimen, which includes bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, has been studied as a standardized treatment course. Modifying this regimen by discontinuing or replacing any of its components prematurely may lead to suboptimal treatment outcomes. According to the pretomanid product label, if either bedaquiline or pretomanid is discontinued, the entire BPaL regimen should also be stopped. If linezolid is permanently discontinued within the first four weeks of treatment, bedaquiline and pretomanid should also be discontinued. However, if linezolid is stopped after the initial four weeks, clinicians should continue administering bedaquiline and pretomanid, following the Nix-TB study protocol, which prescribes 39 weeks of treatment within a 12-month period. Patients who remained culture-positive or reverted to culture-positive status between months four and six, and whose clinical condition suggested ongoing TB infection, had their treatment extended to a total of nine months. Patients receiving the BPaL regimen (or any shorter regimen for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB) require baseline testing and ongoing clinical and laboratory monitoring during treatment. This includes assessing symptoms such as fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, liver tenderness, and hepatomegaly, as well as conducting laboratory tests for liver enzymes (ALT, AST), alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, complete blood count, and serum potassium, calcium, and magnesium levels. Abnormalities in these parameters should be corrected as needed. Clinicians should also obtain an electrocardiogram before initiating treatment. The Nix-TB study employed a more comprehensive baseline monitoring schedule, including a thorough clinical assessment followed by weekly patient monitoring until week 20, and then every four to six weeks thereafter. This schedule depended on whether the patient completed six months of treatment or required an additional three months (totaling nine months). Given that the BPaL regimen is relatively new and implemented under operational research conditions, it is crucial to follow up with patients after treatment completion to monitor for potential relapse. In the Nix-TB study, post-treatment monitoring was conducted monthly for the first three months and then every three months thereafter, for a total of 24 months. However, at the time of data analysis, only about half of the patients had been followed for this duration. Detailed schedules for baseline and follow-up monitoring, including post-treatment follow-up, should be developed for any operational research protocol involving the BPaL regimen. Additional evidence on adverse events will be critical for building a robust safety profile for the BPaL regimen across diverse settings. Monitoring changes in linezolid dosing and duration, when necessary, will also be important for informing future evidence on the broader use of the BPaL regimen and the tolerability of linezolid within this treatment protocol. Research priorities include evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of the BPaL regimen compared to other all-oral regimens, collecting data from regions beyond South Africa, and investigating the mechanisms and molecular markers of pretomanid resistance. Surveillance for resistance development, with attention to the impact of specific mutations, is also essential. Additionally, documenting the full adverse effect profile of pretomanid, particularly its hepatotoxicity and reproductive toxicity in humans, is necessary. While reproductive toxicities have been observed in animal studies, the potential effects on human fertility remain inadequately studied and require further research. Comparative studies on the efficacy of pretomanid versus delamanid, as well as research on the optimal dose and duration of linezolid use in drug-resistant TB regimens (e.g., the ZeNix study), are also needed.
